The bill would strengthen Infrastructure Australia as an independent advisory body on national infrastructure needs, financing, and regulation.
It would re-establish Infrastructure Australia as a separate legal and financial entity under the Commonwealth Authorities and Companies Act 1997.

The bill would more clearly define Infrastructure Australia's functions to improve evidence-based infrastructure planning and prioritisation, with no net budget impact and existing funding of $12.072 million in 2013-14.

Pat Conroy I rise to oppose the Infrastructure Australia Amendment Bill 2013. I follow on from excellent speeches from this side of parliament, which have drawn attention to some very significant flaws in this bill, mostly around the criteria, the granting of extraordinary powers to the minister, the politicisation of an independent process, a complete abandonment of any commitment to an evidence-based approach to infrastructure funding in this country and a clear bias against public transport funding. I would like to concentrate on three particular aspects of this bill, namely the politicisation of a very important process, the impact that this will have on private sector investment and the changes to Infrastructure Australia's role around climate change, which is a little known aspect of this bill and yet another example of the government attacking any independent authority that dares to advise on climate change. Before I go to that, I would like to comment on the proud record that Labor has in this area compared to those opposite. When Labor came to government in 2007 the OECD had ranked Australia 20 out of 25 countries in relation to our investment in public infrastructure as a proportion of national income. I am proud that, because of Labor's record investment-particularly through the GFC, which the member for Scullin highlighted-Australia is now ranked second in the OECD in terms of investment in infrastructure as a percentage of national income. Among the advanced economies only South Korea is investing more in infrastructure. Investment in infrastructure in Australia in 2011-12 was four per cent of GDP, which is the highest it has been in 30 years. Infrastructure Australia Amendment Bill 2013 - in Committee - Local community consultation

Moved the Infrastructure Australia Amendment Bill 2013, which restructures the body established in 2008 into an independent statutory entity with a board and chief executive, requires it to develop a 15-year national infrastructure plan revised every five years, and to review all proposed Commonwealth-funded projects worth more than $100 million.

Opposed the Infrastructure Australia Amendment Bill, said the body he created in 2008 to depoliticise infrastructure decisions would now let the minister nominate or exclude project classes and sack council members, and warned this threatened funding already allocated for projects like the $3 billion Melbourne Metro and $715 million Cross River Rail.

Responded to the member for Grayndler, accused Labor of its own pork-barrelling record through Regional Development Australia grants for projects with no regional links, such as a sports complex in Wyndham, a swimming pool in Ringwood and funding for the Penrith football club, all in metropolitan areas.

Supported the bill, listing major coalition infrastructure commitments including $6.7 billion for the Bruce Highway and $5.6 billion to complete the Pacific Highway duplication, and highlighted a local flood mitigation project near Patties Foods in Bairnsdale, a business that has grown from a family cake shop 45 years ago into a company turning over $250 million a year.

Opposed the bill, said it removes the requirement that ministerial directions to Infrastructure Australia be of a general nature only, noted Labor had doubled federal infrastructure spending per capita from $141 to $269 and total investment was 40 per cent higher in real terms than under the previous coalition government, and warned funding had been withdrawn from Brisbane's Cross River Rail project, needed to add capacity for 17,000 more peak-time passengers.

Supported the bill, said the coalition's total infrastructure package exceeds $20 billion including almost $5 billion in additional funding, criticised Labor's $2 billion pre-election promise for the Parramatta-Epping Rail Link that never qualified for Infrastructure Australia assessment, and welcomed a new requirement for published cost-benefit analyses on projects worth over $100 million.

Supported the bill, highlighted the government's inland rail project from Melbourne to Brisbane, to be led by an implementation group chaired by former Deputy Prime Minister John Anderson, noted a stalled Howard-era commitment of $500 million a year for the M1 upgrade near his electorate, and said nearby growth areas expect about 200,000 more residents over the next 30 years without adequate public transport.

Opposed the bill, accused the government of reducing Infrastructure Australia's independence and transparency, recounted an anecdote of a National Party state minister secretly reprioritising a road to favour his own farm, and credited Labor's 2007 election commitment for finally securing federal funding for Pilbara roads into Karratha and Port Hedland.

Supported the bill, said the $5.6 billion commitment to complete the Pacific Highway between Ballina and Woolgoolga occurred despite Infrastructure Australia rather than because of it, criticised the previous government for cutting its funding split with New South Wales once the state government changed hands, and welcomed the new government's recommitment to an 80 per cent federal funding share.

Opposed the Infrastructure Australia Amendment Bill 2013, citing Labor's record of investing $64 billion in infrastructure including $13.6 billion in urban public transport, and detailed the $2.8 billion Ipswich Motorway upgrade from Dinmore to Darra compared with the coalition's reduced $65 million offer for its final Darra to Rocklea section.

Opposed the Infrastructure Australia Amendment Bill 2013, comparing its rhetoric of transparency to the Work Choices legislation, and recalled former Prime Minister Howard's declaration that 'we don't do infrastructure' as evidence of the coalition's historical neglect of the sector.

Opposed the bill, recounting the Howard-era 'regional rorts' scandal in which 28 of 32 funded projects went to coalition electorates, including a $5 million grant for a Beaudesert tourist railway that went bankrupt, and contrasted Infrastructure Australia's endorsement of Melbourne Metro with the Prime Minister's $1.5 billion pledge to the East-West Link before seeing its business case.

Opposed the Infrastructure Australia Amendment Bill 2013, noting Australia's OECD ranking for infrastructure investment rose from 20th out of 25 countries in 2007 to second under Labor, with spending reaching 4 per cent of GDP in 2011-12, the highest level in 30 years.
Raised a point of order disputing the Speaker's declaration that a vote had carried, and insisted on being permitted to speak to his amendment to the Infrastructure Australia Amendment Bill.

The speaker moved a motion to change committee memberships, discharging Senator Urquhart and appointing Senator Gallacher to the National Disability Insurance Scheme Joint Standing Committee, and appointing substitute members for several other committees including Wright, Milne, and Ludlam.

Moved that the Senate's amendments to the Infrastructure Australia Amendment Bill be agreed, accepting most changes while flagging concerns some add unnecessary red tape, and said the government wants Infrastructure Australia to scrutinise every project valued at more than $100 million.

Argued that Labor supports the amendments to the Infrastructure Australia Amendment Bill, saying the original bill would have let the minister exclude categories of infrastructure such as public transport, and cited funding cuts to the Cross River Rail and Melbourne Metro projects as evidence of that risk.
